zones.label: Column 1

It is a contextual cross-check, not the authority for this scan's letters, accents, or typography. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: The opening continuation ends a comparison gloss. Furui kotodomo hikidaite introduces bringing forward old matters as parallels; fiqidai- continues on the next physical row.
Sore ni tague means comparing those old matters with that case. The weakened r in ſoreni is read with the Japanese construction; Feiq. is the citation label, followed by the italic book reference.

The Portuguese translates the example as bringing forward old things and comparing them. The a in Trazendo is abraded; the surviving word and its participial function support this reading rather than Truzendo.
A isso completes the comparison with the matter at hand. This short italic continuation is a complete physical row, not a new entry.
Tajimeki describes unsteady movement while weak or injured. The Portuguese feri- continues as ferido below; the abbreviated Japanese principal forms are retained rather than modernized.

runs.text: do não ſe poder ter em pè, nem caminhar ſegura-

lines.note: The injured or weakened person cannot remain standing or walk securely. The scan supports nem, not nent; segura- belongs to seguramente on the next row.
Mente completes seguramente, qualifying the inability to walk steadily. It is not independent lexical material.

Tajiroki means moving or wavering. The first Portuguese capital has an E-like outline in this impression, although bulir-se is clearly the intended synonym of mover-se; Eulirſe is retained as a graphic anomaly, not silently regularized to Bulirſe.
Ashi ga tajiroku describes the feet trembling or moving unsteadily. Bulirem supplies a clear local comparison for the intended sense of the preceding damaged gloss.

runs.text: os pẽs como quem quer cair. ¶ Item, per

lines.note: The feet move as though the person were about to fall. Per begins the dictionary's transition to a metaphorical sense on the next row; the small mark in pẽs remains a diplomatic uncertainty.

runs.text: met. Moſt arſe inconſtante, & fraco nas

lines.note: The metaphorical sense is showing oneself inconstant and weak. The print is damaged in expected mostrar-se; the visibly separated Moſt arſe is retained pending any human reading of the missing-looking stroke rather than supplying a secure r.
The figurative gloss concerns important matters. Nangui idequ- begins a concessive example about difficulties arising; the word is idekuru, not the misleading fused hint Nanguiadequ.
Redomo completes the concessive form: although hardships arise, faith does not waver. Fidesua joins Latin fides to Japanese wa; the Portuguese translation begins here and continues below.

With the preceding a, this says that hardships occurred, yet the person did not doubt. Several types are abraded; the context supports contecerão and trabalhos, while the visibly short todaua is retained rather than silently adding the expected i of todauia.

runs.text: nem ſe moueo nas couſas da Fè.

lines.note: The person did not shift in matters of faith. This completes the metaphorical example, with historical moueo and Fè retained.
Tajitajito is an adverb describing weak, faltering movement. The next short row completes the comparison with falling.
The faltering walk is compared to falling. The phrase completes Tagitagito and remains separate from the following Tai entries.
This Tai denotes substance or underlying body. It is an independent homograph, not the fish or desiderative ending defined below.
This Tai is the fish, compared with a sea bream. The Portuguese comparison supplies the identification without requiring a modern species name.
Tai is given with the preferable form taimatsu, a torch. The Latin potiùs belongs to the apparatus; the material description continues on the next row. The headword closes with a point, not a comma.

runs.text: de pinho, de bambùs ſecos, ou outra couſa.

lines.note: The torch is made from pine splints, dry bamboo, or another material. Bambùs retains its printed accent and the historical plural spelling.

runs.text: Querer, ou deſejar. Quer eſta palaura

lines.note: The ending -tai expresses wanting or desiring. Quer begins the grammatical instruction that this element requires a verb in its stem form; it is not OCR Ques.

runs.text: o verbo na raiz, & cõjugaſe polla conjuga-

lines.note: The dictionary attaches -tai to the verb stem and says that it inflects like an adjective. The weakened middle of cõjugaſe is read as the grammatical verb, retaining its abbreviation tilde.
This completes the adjective-inflection explanation and introduces yomitai, wanting to read. The following i introduces an equivalent expression, not part of the Japanese word.
Yomitō gozaru is the alternative desiderative expression, translated as wanting to read. The caron in the contracted adjective is visible; the malformed hint Yonaitǒgozaru is rejected.
Tai-aku is explained as driving away evil, here withdrawing from sins. The gloss's worn consonants are read as afaſtarſe; this is not an instruction to modernize the Japanese expression.
The phrase completes withdrawal from sins. Tai aku shuzen pairs abandoning evil with practising goodness, and its Portuguese explanation begins with Deixar.
The paired action is abandoning wickedness and giving oneself to virtue. The final upright S. labels written usage rather than continuing the italic sentence.
Taibyō means a great or serious illness, matched by ōkina yamai. The damaged headword remains a single word; the scan supports the internal bi rather than the OCR's separated Ta biǒ.

This entry concerns a great desire or aspiration. Enlargement leaves a u+n-like sequence in the alternative, so taunǒ is retained as the adopted graphic reading. The supplied NINJAL entry gives taimǒ, a useful lexical identification but not sufficient evidence to replace this impression's damaged letterforms.
De completes Grande across the physical break, giving great desire. The upright S. is the written-register label.
This Taibô denotes a great scheme or stratagem, with the closed-o circumflex distinct from the preceding aspiration entry's caron. The Portuguese noun ardil continues with a synonym below.

Inuenção completes the stratagem gloss, followed by the written-register label. The far-right aruore is displaced text belonging semantically to the next entry's large tree; it stays on this physical row with explicit placement, not attached to the invention gloss. The cedilla beneath ç is visible on reinspection.
Taiboku is a large tree or piece of timber, matching ōkina ki. Its last Portuguese alternative is the displaced aruore on the preceding row; no accent is secure on the final u of Taibocu.
Taika, alternatively taika no hito, denotes a great or noble person. The Japanese alternative is not Portuguese prose and is not marked as an embedded typeface term.
Muito nobre completes the noble-person definition. The damaged vowel in muito is supported by the remaining strokes and the phrase, not the OCR reading meito.
Taikan means opposing or resisting, paraphrased by mukai kobamu. The m of cobamu replaces the OCR's malformed n-r sequence; the Portuguese re- continues below.
The example is resisting one's master, shujin ni taikan suru. The two adjacent n types in Xujinni represent the noun-final n and the particle, not the OCR's extra m.
Ir à mão is explained by resisting the master. The two s letters in reſiſtir are distinct from the following t; the historical idiom is retained.
Taichū denotes great service or loyalty. The example repeats the headword with object particle uo and starts nasu, completed below; both long-u marks are retained as carons.
Su completes nasu, to perform great services. The right-aligned eſtima belongs semantically to the next definition, not this sentence; its physical location is preserved as a displaced span.

runs.text: Couſa grande, ou alta, ou de

lines.note: Taikō and taikōna describe something great, lofty, or esteemed. The Portuguese ends with de and takes the displaced eſtima on the preceding row; the alternative is taicǒna, not OCR cacǒni.
This homograph is a great rope, glossed by ōzuna. The following explanation extends the image to fundamental bonds and rules.

runs.text: ſta palaura he mais metaphorico, per leis, ou pre

lines.note: With the preceding de, ſta completes desta. The word is chiefly metaphorical, referring to laws or precepts; mais is restored from the visible type, and the line-end pre is left without an invented hyphen.

runs.text: ceitos principaes, ou ſustanciaes, ou vinculo

lines.note: Ceitos completes preceitos: principal or essential precepts, or a binding connection. The printed spelling and s-allograph in ſustanciaes are retained.

runs.text: cõque algũs eſtados de gẽte eſtão ẽtre ſi liados

lines.note: The bond ties certain classes or conditions of people to one another. The phrase is entre si liados, with abbreviation tildes preserved; the OCR's final ltados is not supported.
Master and servant, husband and wife are the examples of mutually bound social relations. The right-edge &c. is included rather than lost after the damaged molher.

runs.text: Couſa de grande alegria, & bom ſuc

lines.note: This taikō concerns great joy and good fortune. The Portuguese sucesso is divided across rows; the right edge is retained without supplying a secure hyphen where the impression is weak.
Ceßo completes successo in the gloss of good fortune. The final upright S. marks written usage.
Taikō here means great meritorious services, equated with ōkina chūkō. The circumflexes distinguish it graphically from the preceding joy entry; chǔcô corrects the damaged OCR chicô.
Taikō wo tsumu means accumulating great services or merits. The Portuguese Acumular has a weak middle, but the repetition and definition support the reading; ſer- continues below.
Uiços completes ſeruiços, the services accumulated in the preceding example. The initial u remains historical Portuguese typography, not modern v.
Taiko is a drum, explained by ōkina tsuzumi. The repeated example begins Tai- and continues on the following row, distinct from the long-vowel service entry.
The example gives sounding or striking the drum. The complete Portuguese phrase, including its initial T, is italic; the Japanese alternatives remain roman.
Taikoku is a great country or kingdom, matching ōkina kuni. The worn middle of the headword is read as cocu, not the OCR's separated Tuito u.
The adjectival form taikōna refers back to Taicǒ. Vide is italic apparatus; the referenced Japanese word is roman and is an eligible whole-word typeface term.
Taikōni is adverbial; taikōni zonzuru means holding something in high esteem. The repeated form ends in ni, not OCR ui.
The translation completes the idea of holding or valuing something highly. The printed s form in estimar is left unchanged.
Taikutsu is weariness or boredom, with a literal explanatory pair of withdrawing and bending. Enfadamento requires f, not long s; the Portuguese word is continued semantically below.
Fastio specifies aversion or weariness toward something. Taikutsu suru introduces becoming bored; the Portuguese infinitive is divided En- / fadarſe.
This completes Enfadarſe, becoming weary or bored. The initial f is part of that verb, not an independent long-s word.

runs.text: Grandes paços reaes que ouue anti-

lines.note: Taidairi names the former great imperial palace complex. The Portuguese refers to royal palaces that existed in earlier times, with antiguamente divided across rows.

runs.text: guamente, à maneira de cidade cercada.

lines.note: The palace complex resembled an enclosed city. This completes the historical description rather than adding a separate headword.
Taidan means meeting to speak or consult, paraphrased by mukai kataru. The nasal abbreviation cõ- begins consultar at the next line.

runs.text: ſultar com alguem ſobre algũ negocio. ¶

lines.note: The consultation concerns some business. The repeated Taidan example is physically divided Tai- / dan and must not be joined in the diplomatic text.
The future expressions offer to meet or confer later. The scan's first vowel in mosǒzu is too worn to add a secure length mark; the printed future ending and the alternative itasǒzu remain legible.
The Portuguese says that they will meet later and discuss matters. Depois is one printed word, rather than the OCR split de pois.
Taiha means great waves, matching ōkina nami. The rounded initial of ondas corrects OCR endas; S. is an upright written-use label.

This homograph means great destruction. The weakened explanatory form is retained as Vôqiri rather than automatically changed to a familiar adverb; yaburu and the Portuguese establish the destructive sense.
Taiha ni oyobu means reaching a state of great destruction. The pilcrow is visibly present and restored; de- begins the divided Portuguese noun.
Struição completes destruição. The t and r are present despite the draft's defective ſouição.

runs.text: Certas boninas, ou flores brancas do

lines.note: Taihaku is described as a kind of white flower. The dictionary's descriptive gloss is preserved without assigning a more precise botanical species.
The flowers bloom in autumn and are very large and beautiful. This completes the floral entry, retaining historical fermoſas.

runs.text: Certas corteſias, & ceremonias q̃ fazẽ os

lines.note: Taihai concerns formal manners and ceremonies performed by archers. The abbreviation q̃ and the nasal ending of fazẽ remain unexpanded.

runs.text: q̃ tirão ao arco ẽ por o joelho no chaõ, no tomar do

lines.note: The explanation mentions bowmen putting the knee on the ground and taking up the bow. The printed separate por o and the abbreviation ẽ are retained; arco is not fused with the following preposition.
The example taihai ga yoi praises the archer's carriage or deportment. The Portuguese word is meneo, movement or bearing, not the draft's menco; cõpo- continues below.

runs.text: ſição, &c. do q̃ tira cõ arco he boa, & airoſa.

lines.note: The archer's bearing and composure are good and graceful. This completes composição and retains the printed abbreviations rather than expanding them.
A second taihai entry describes bodily proportion or physical arrangement. Its Portuguese gloss continues with humano below, not with the preceding archery example.
The definition first concerns the human body, then extends to the proportion and shape of an object named on the next row.
The second sense concerns the shape of a katana. Butaihai no mono then introduces a person of poor bearing; the headword fragment has t rather than the OCR's c, and the final word is mono, not monc.
The person is negligent in appearance and of poor bodily bearing. The Portuguese describes the negative example from the preceding line.
The definition adds ill-bred or badly brought up. This is a continuation of Butaifaino mono, not a new entry.
Taihan is the greater part or the majority, equated here with tairyaku. Amayor preserves the printed joined spelling; pola- continues below.

The gloss says for the most part, though porte is the visible printed form rather than expected parte. Tenka no taihan wo tamochi introduces holding the greater part of the realm; its worn n is read with the repeated entry.
Chi completes tamochi, holding or possessing. The Portuguese confirms possession of the greater part of the empire and retains joined amayor.

Taihei is tranquillity or peace, explained by being broadly at ease. The damaged headword's f and the intact following examples correct the OCR's separated Ta fei; the Portuguese word continues below.
The definition completes tranquillity and peace. Tenka wo taihei ni osamuru means governing the realm peacefully; the example's f is not r, and the verb is divided across rows.
Muru completes osamuru. The Portuguese translates the whole example as governing the empire in peace.

runs.text: Grãdes bulles como fraſcos de vinho.

lines.note: This homograph names large vessels resembling wine flasks. The worn f matches the adjacent Taifei family and is not the OCR's r; bulles and the abbreviation in Grãdes are retained.

Taiheiki is identified as a book of Japanese histories. The final country name reads Iapão, not Iação; its upright types contrast with the italic preceding explanation. Iapão is Portuguese, so it is not marked as a Japanese embedded term.
Taihen, alternatively taihenna, describes something very great or involving much business. The repeated alternative helps interpret the abraded f in the headword.
The definition adds a matter involving much business or a laborious thing. Couſa is the noun thing here, not the draft's cauſa.
Taihenni is the adverbial form; taihenni omou means considering something a great or troublesome matter. Both repeated forms are read against the print rather than the malformed kana hint.
The Portuguese completes the example: regarding something as great or laborious. The right edge ends with a period, distinct from the catchword below.
